wrong: Research exploring experiences through interviews
That is qualitative research, which studies meanings rather than numbers.
Research describing one case in great detail
That is a case study.
Research based on observing people in natural settings
That is field observation, usually a qualitative method.
Research measuring variables with numbers
That is quantitative research.
Research testing hypotheses statistically
Statistical hypothesis testing is quantitative research.
Research using large random surveys
Large structured surveys produce numerical data, which is typical of quantitative research.
Survey of a large sample
That is survey research, which studies many cases briefly.
Controlled test of a treatment group
That is an experiment.
Count of crimes in an area
That is crime statistics, not a case study.
Rate of crimes solved by police
That is the clearance rate.
Rate of cases ending in conviction
That is the conviction rate.
Rate of first-time offending
That is the rate of first offenses; recidivism is repeat offending.
Captors develop sympathy for their hostages
That is the Lima syndrome, the reverse of Stockholm syndrome.
Hostages feel lasting fear after release
That describes trauma, such as PTSD.
Negotiators bond with the hostage-taker
Negotiators build rapport on purpose; Stockholm syndrome is about the hostages.
Focus on deterring others through punishment
That is deterrence.
Focus on removing offenders from society
That is incapacitation.
Focus on punishment the offender deserves
That is retribution, or just deserts.
Using force to end a disagreement
Force may end a dispute but does not resolve it peacefully.
Avoiding the problem until it goes away
Avoidance leaves the conflict unresolved.
Letting the stronger party decide the outcome
That is domination, not resolution.
Reforming offenders
That is rehabilitation, which works on the offender rather than the situation.
Harsher prison terms
That is deterrence through the law, not situational prevention.
Fixing root social causes
That is social or developmental prevention.
Building more prisons to hold offenders
That is incapacitation, not environmental design.
Patrolling streets with more police
That is police presence, not environmental design.
Painting murals on walls
Murals are art projects; CPTED changes the design of spaces to reduce crime.
Punishing the offender in proportion to the harm
That is retribution.
Isolating the offender to protect the community
That is incapacitation.
Deterring the public through visible punishment
That is general deterrence.
Person victimized only once
That is a one-time victim, the opposite of a repeat victim.
Person who saw a crime twice
A witness is not a victim.
Offender who was once a victim
That describes the overlap between victims and offenders.
Fine paid by the offender to the state
A fine goes to the government, not to the victim.
Free legal counsel for the accused
That is legal aid for the accused, not help for the victim.
Payment to witnesses for testifying
Witnesses are not paid to testify; compensation programs aid victims.

wrong: Biological traits of the offender
That is the positivist view of Lombroso.
Influence of the social environment
That is sociological positivism.
Economic need and lack of opportunity
Economic explanations belong to positivist and strain theories, not the classical school.
Crime is a rational choice by the offender
That is the classical school.
Crime is caused by evil spirits
That is demonological thinking, which came before scientific criminology.
Crime is weighed as pleasure versus pain
That is Bentham's hedonistic calculus, part of the classical school.
All criminals learn crime from others
That is differential association.
Crime is chosen after weighing pleasure and pain
That is the classical school.
Labels from society create career criminals
That is labeling theory.
Study of the role of victims
That is victimology.
Study of punishment and prisons
That is penology.
Study of how laws are made
That is the sociology of law.
Serious crime committed by a minor
Serious crimes are illegal at any age; status offenses apply only to minors.
Offense punished more for adults
Status offenses are acts that are not crimes at all for adults.
Crime that depends on social status
Despite the name, it is not about social class; it is about the status of being a minor.

wrong: Transfer of the child to an adult jail
RA 9344 prohibits detaining children together with adults.
Suspension of sentence after a guilty finding
That is suspended sentence, which happens after a finding of guilt, not instead of court.
Dismissal of the case with no program
Diversion still requires a program the child must complete.
Suspension of sentence after conviction
That is suspended sentence, which happens after a finding of guilt.
Confinement in a regular jail cell
Children may not be detained with adults; diversion avoids formal proceedings.
Automatic dismissal without conditions
Diversion comes with a program the child must complete.
Law Enforcement, Prosecution, Courts, Corrections, Legislature
Congress makes the laws but is not a pillar; the fifth pillar is the community.
Law Enforcement, Prosecution, Defense, Courts, Corrections
The defense is not a separate pillar; the fifth pillar is the community.
Investigation, Trial, Verdict, Punishment, Rehabilitation
These are stages of a case, not the pillars.
Loyalty to fellow officers
Blind loyalty can lead to covering up misconduct; integrity is adherence to ethics.
Strict obedience to any order
Integrity requires refusing unlawful orders.
Popularity with the public
Integrity is not about popularity.
Choice between obeying the law and breaking it for gain
That is a temptation, not a dilemma, because the right answer is clear.
Situation with only one clearly right answer
A dilemma has no clearly right answer; both choices rest on moral principles.
Disagreement over which rule applies to a case
That is a legal question, not a conflict between moral principles.
Merton's Strain Theory
Merton's strain theory says crime comes from blocked access to goals.
Labeling Theory
Labeling theory says reactions to deviance push people into more crime.
General Theory of Crime (self-control)
Gottfredson and Hirschi say crime comes from low self-control formed in childhood.
Labels deter people from committing crime
Labeling theory argues the reverse: the label pushes people toward more crime.
Crime is learned from close associates
That is differential association.
Weak social bonds free people to offend
That is social control theory.
Pressure from blocked goals causes crime
That is strain theory.
Criminal labels push people into crime
That is labeling theory.
Crime is learned from close associates
That is differential association.
Crime is inherited from criminal parents
That is a biological explanation.
Crime results from weak social bonds
That is social control theory.
Crime comes from blocked goals
That is strain theory.
Mood disorder with deep sadness
That is depression.
Psychosis with loss of reality
Psychopaths are typically in touch with reality; psychosis is a different condition.
Anxiety disorder with intense fear
That is an anxiety disorder.
Antisocial personality present from birth through genes
That is how psychopathy is often described; sociopathy is linked more to environment.
Mental illness marked by hallucinations and delusions
That describes psychosis, such as schizophrenia.
Extreme shyness and intense fear of social situations
That is social anxiety.
Total of all crimes reported
The index counts only selected serious (index) crimes.
Count of petty crimes only
Petty crimes are non-index crimes.
Number of crimes solved
That is the clearance count.
Biological approach to crime
That is the Italian (positivist) school.
Free will approach to crime
That is the classical school.
Psychoanalytic approach to criminal behavior
That is the Freudian approach.
Crime is inherited through genes from criminal parents
That is a biological explanation.
Crime results from strain between goals and legitimate means
That is strain theory.
Crime is a rational choice after weighing the costs and benefits
That is rational choice theory.
Ronald Akers
Akers built social learning theory on Sutherland's work.
Edwin Lemert
Lemert introduced primary and secondary deviance in labeling theory.
Michael Gottfredson
Gottfredson co-wrote the General Theory of Crime (self-control) with Hirschi.
